Summary

Executive Summary

Of the 4,330 jobs the shop released in 2025, 45% earned more than the 22% target margin, 13% landed within two points of it, 42% fell below it and 8% lost money. The 1,839 jobs below target fell $2.21M short of target contribution (96% of the cost measured). Two cost elements carry most of that: run hours over estimate ($1.47M) and outside processing over estimate ($343K). The largest named causes are revision work at one customer that was worked and never billed ($545K) and titanium and Inconel jobs that ran well past their estimated run hours ($395K); $775K of the overrun has no cause the data can name. The decisions the owner took during the engagement act on causes that account for $1.54M, 49% of the gross shortfall before offsets. The rest has no cause the data can name, sits in quotes and vendor prices no decision has reached yet, or is a cost the owner declined to act on; Section 10 lists the decisions both ways. What the job-level comparison showed, and the P&L could not, is that the year's 24.3% average was an average of jobs running from a loss to well over target, and that the same part could do both in the same year.

Section 1

Situation

Before the engagement the shop could see three things about margin: the gross margin on the monthly P&L, the estimate on each quote line, and the standing price on each repeat part. It could not see what any job actually cost. The ERP's job costing module had never been configured, so no job carried its estimate, and labor, material, outside processing and scrap were recorded without being assembled into a job's cost.

It can now. Every job carries its estimate and its actual cost by element (material, setup hours, run hours, outside processing, scrap and rework), built from the transactions, and every job states how much of its cost is measured rather than estimated. For the 2025 jobs this report reads, 96% of the cost is measured; on the jobs completed under the new process, 99%. All figures cost labor at each work center's own rate (its rate pool), not the shop's single blended rate; why that matters is in the data quality audit, error #2, One Blended Shop Rate.

Section 3

Anatomy of the Shortfall

Every 2025 job that landed below target is taken apart the same way. Its shortfall, the contribution it would have earned at the target margin less the contribution it did earn, splits exactly into two parts: the price set against the estimate, and the actual cost over the estimate, element by element. The estimate is re-costed at today's prices first (its hours at the job's own pool rate, its material at the part's need at the job's issue price), so the labor elements are hours and the material element is usage; what prices moved since the quote sits in the price line, where the repricing queue picks it up.

Across the 1,839 below-target jobs the shortfall is $2.21M (96% of the cost measured). Run hours over estimate are the largest element by a wide margin, followed by outside processing and setup hours. The price line is negative in total: on average these jobs were priced above target at the estimate, so the shortfall came from what the jobs took rather than from what they were quoted at.

Section 3.1

Run hours over estimate

Run hours are over estimate almost everywhere a little, and in titanium and Inconel a lot. The little is stoppages: a job's run hours include the alarms and in-operation idle the machines record, 30% of machine time, and the routing standard carries no allowance for them. Standards set generously at first quote absorb part of it (before the refresh they sat a median 9% above the measured cycle), so the median job runs 1.09× its estimated run hours. Jobs in the two alloys ran 1.31× their estimated run hours in 2025 against 1.09× for every other material, and the gap shows on every cell that cuts them, which says the estimate is wrong rather than the floor: the estimator's speeds and feeds for the two alloys were never checked against a measured cycle. On the below-target jobs the excess over the shop's normal overrun comes to 1,878 hours and $395K across 165 jobs (99% of the cost measured). The action is to validate the two alloys' speeds and feeds against the measured cycles.

Two further causes sit in run hours. Parts whose routing standard was below the cycle the machines measured ran over the estimate by the difference until the standard was refreshed: $162K on 545 jobs. And the two oldest vertical mills, installed in 2006 and 2008, run the same program 1.26× as long as the newer ones on the 588 parts that ran on both; a job the schedule put on one of them carried that difference, $85K on 303 below-target jobs.

Section 3.2

Setup hours over estimate

Setup overruns concentrate in small lots on the mill-turn and 5-axis cells. Measured at the cell against the routing standard, setup on lots under 25 pieces runs 1.62× the standard against 1.04× on larger lots: the standard assumes a repeat setup and a small lot gets a first-article setup every time. Margin by lot size shows the result, falling off sharply below 25 pieces rather than gradually.

Margin by Lot Size, with Setup Hours against Standard on the Mill-turn and 5-axis Cells, 2025

On the below-target jobs the setup excess on those cells comes to $39K across 123 jobs (98% of the cost measured); the first run after a revision adds $20K on 37 jobs, the same first-article effect on a part the shop already knew. The action is to quote small lots at the measured first-article setup.

Section 3.3

Labor hours over estimate with no routing cause

One customer's jobs run over on labor across every part family they buy. Mendoza-Davis jobs averaged 8.2 labor hours over estimate per job in 2025, against 0.3 for every other customer; in total they ran 1.27× their estimated hours against 1.01×. Nothing in the routing explains it: the excess shows on every part family the customer buys. The explanation is on the customer record. Mendoza-Davis issued 41 revision changes in the last twelve months against a median of 3 across the book, and each one adds programming and first-article time after release that was never billed.

Section 3.4

Outside processing over estimate

Outside processing over estimate has three parts. The plating vendor is the clearest case: it raised its prices in steps while the estimator's spreadsheet kept the old rate, so the gap between invoice and estimate widened quarter by quarter: on jobs whose only outside process is plating, the invoice ran 1.34× the estimate through 2025, and fell back to 1.03× once the quoting module carried the vendor's current price.

Plating: Invoice over Estimate by Quarter Released, Jobs Plated and Nothing Else

On the below-target plated jobs that cost $32K. Other vendors' invoices above the estimate add more in total, $227K, but thinly: a median of $58 a job across 1,066 jobs, the drift of vendor prices since the job was quoted. The third part, $178K, is outside processing that could never be tied to a job and was spread over the month's jobs so the ledger reconciles; it is real money, but where it landed is an allocation, not a measurement. The action is to carry current vendor pricing in the quoting module; with a job number now required on every outside-processing purchase order, the comparison runs itself.

Section 3.5

Scrap and rework

Scrap material and rework hours cost the below-target jobs $76K, led by stainless fittings ($13K) and aerospace brackets ($11K). The figure is a floor: before the engagement most rework was posted as run time (881 events the audit found), so part of it sits in the run-hours line above and can only be partly separated after the fact.

Section 3.6

Material

Material usage is small, as it should be once issues are costed at their own price: $14K net across the below-target jobs. What remains is the remnant and mis-issue cases the audit corrected (2,734 jobs that received another job's bar or never had theirs issued, brought back to the part's need).

Same Part, Different Outcomes

For quoting this means one thing: a part's price has to cover its worst realistic job, not its average. A standing price set on the typical lot on the newer machine loses money whenever the release is small, the schedule puts the job on an older mill or the customer revises the part, and each of those happens several times a year on the same part numbers.

Section 5

Jobs That Could Have Been Caught in Progress

The job in progress screen flags a job when its actual to date runs more than 15% over its estimate to date on labor hours, operation by operation, or on material at issue. Replayed over the 4,330 jobs completed from the 2025 releases, 1,279 would have been flagged, and 613 of them while there was still something to do: with operations left and 3 or more days before the job shipped. 33% of the flags fire at the first operation, where setup overruns show, 63% at a middle operation and 4% at the last, when only the next quote can change.

Where on the Routing the Flag Fired, 2025 Jobs

Grouped by what the shop could have done with the warning: on Mendoza-Davis's jobs a change order could have been raised before the work was done; on jobs that went on to ship late, a flag at the first operation leaves time to re-sequence rather than expedite; on small lots and first runs after a revision the quantity or scope could have been discussed with the customer. The three groups carried $1.29M of cost over estimate across 405 jobs. The rest were flagged too late or had no lever while open.

What the flag allowedJobsCost over estimateMedian days before shipCost measured
Change order billed173$548K496%
Expedite avoided191$711K598%

Nothing: no lever while open208$256K494%

This is what the shop could have known while the jobs were open, not what it would have recovered. A flag is a conversation, and the conversation does not always go the shop's way.

Section 8

Repricing

Exposure. At today's material prices, pool rates and measured standards, 246 of the 1,600 repeat parts (15%) have a standing price below current cost plus target, carrying 12% of repeat revenue. The gap is modest on most of them: a median of 5.4%, with nine in ten under 15%; 4 sit below cost outright. At current volume the exposure is $256K a year, and the own-product line adds $326K: together 1.0% of 2025 revenue. Current cost rests on measured standards on 100% of the parts. The gap is what the annual across-the-board letters (3.0% to 3.5% a year) missed on the parts whose inputs moved most: since the last quote, current cost rose a median 21% on the parts below target against 1% on the rest, while the letters raised the standing prices of those parts a median 11%.

What is defensible. In the shop's experience, as the owner and the controller described it, a routine annual increase of 3 to 5% is accepted without discussion. A larger increase can land selectively, part by part, when the cost driver is documented, and most often that driver is material passed through at what it now costs. Beyond that the relationship risk is real, and the owner decides.

Decisions. The controller and the owner decided every part below target in weeks 7 to 9 on that basis: a gap within the routine range was repriced; a larger gap was repriced where material or outside processing drove it and the movement could be shown part by part, and held otherwise with the reason recorded; a large gap on a small part was exited, and on the 7 largest programs the increase was taken in two steps, half now and the balance at the blanket renewal.

Section 9

Estimate Accuracy

Estimate accuracy is the distribution of actual over estimate by cost element, for the 2025 history (estimates backfilled from the quoting module) and for the completed jobs of the engagement period (estimate carried on the job). This is the feedback loop the shop never had: the estimator can now see, element by element, whether the quotes were right.

Actual over Estimate by Element, 2025 History against the Engagement Period

Material moved to 1.00 and its spread closed because the estimate now carries the price of the day rather than the spreadsheet's price list. Setup hours have not moved yet (a median of 0.81 against 0.85): 40% of the engagement-period jobs were estimated before their part's refreshed standard took effect, and small lots still run over, which is what action A6 is for. Run hours narrowed from 0.97 to 1.28 to 1.02 to 1.24 because repeat parts are now estimated on the measured cycle. The median stays at 1.11 for a reason the refresh cannot fix: the measured cycle is time in cycle, while a job's run hours also carry the alarms and in-operation idle the machines record, 30% of machine time. The standard needs an allowance for them. Labor and burden tightened further because the estimate and the actual now use the same pool rate. Outside processing moved to 1.02 because the quoting module carries the vendors' current prices.

By estimator, the gap between the margin expected and the margin realized runs 2 to 4 points, about the same for all three: the shortfall is in what the estimates carry, not in who writes them. By quote year, the realized margin on new work has not improved on its own, from 22% on work quoted in 2023 to 18% on work quoted in 2026; that is what the feedback loop is for.

Appendix

Method, Definitions and Detail

Job cost. Material at the issued price, corrected to the part's need where the audit found another job's bar or none; labor as hours at the work center's pool rate (labor rate × attended ratio + burden); outside processing at the invoiced price, with lines that could not be tied to a job allocated over the month's jobs; scrap at the job's material cost. CNC hours come from the machine-monitoring feed on every monitored cell, not from the clock record.

Measured share. The share of a job's cost resting on a transaction (a machine interval assigned to the job, a clock record, a scan, an issue, a purchase order) rather than on the routing standard, an allocated ledger residual or a record flagged unrepairable. Stated beside every dollar figure as the coverage of the jobs behind it.

Margin conventions. Markup on cost is the quoting convention (target 28%); margin on price is the reporting convention (target 22%). A job is on target within 2 points of 22%, below target under that and losing money below zero.

Shortfall and its split. A below-target job's shortfall is target margin times price less its contribution. It splits exactly into the price line (target contribution less the contribution the estimate promised, with the estimate re-costed at today's prices) and the actual over the re-costed estimate by element. A cause is sized as the excess over what a normal 2025 job shows: titanium and Inconel run hours beyond the median run ratio of other materials; small-lot and first-run setup beyond the median setup ratio of larger lots; Mendoza-Davis's hours beyond the shop's median labor ratio; the older mills' run hours times one less the ratio of newer to older cycle; standards below the measured cycle by the gap in the refresh log, on jobs estimated before the refresh.

In-progress flag. A job is flagged at the first operation where its labor hours to date exceed the estimate to date by more than 15% and by at least two hours, or at the first material issue if material exceeds the estimate by more than 15% and $150. The estimate to date is the routing standard for each operation, scaled so the operations sum to the job's estimated hours. A flag is actionable when it fires before the last operation and 3 or more days before the job ships.
